<<Historical Context of the Split>>  
The schism between Sunni and Shi'a Muslims began in the early 7th century during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman. While the caliphate was initially unified, the conflict over the succession to the Prophet Muhammad's leadership emerged. The Umayyad caliphs (661–750) established the caliphate, claiming legitimacy through hereditary succession, while the Abbasids (750–1258) rejected this, advocating for election of the caliph. The schism deepened during the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE, when Imam Hussein, the Prophet's grandson, was martyred, symbolizing the Shi'a belief in the Imamate. This event marked the rise of Shi'a Islam as a distinct sect, emphasizing the importance of the Ahl al-Bayt (family of the Prophet) and the Imamate.  

<<Theological Differences: Imamate vs. Caliphate>>  
The core theological distinction lies in the concept of the Imamate. Sunnis reject the idea of an Imam, asserting that the Prophet Muhammad's caliphate was divinely ordained through election, not heredity. They view the caliph as a political leader chosen by the community, with the caliphate being a temporary institution. In contrast, Shi'a believe in the divine right of the Imam to lead the community, with the Imam being a spiritual and political leader chosen by the Ahl al-Bayt. The Shi'a also believe in the "Twelve Imams," a lineage of spiritual leaders who are considered infallible and divinely appointed. The governance structure of Sunni and Shi'a Islam differs significantly. Sunnis believe in the caliphate as a divine institution, where the caliph is the leader of the Muslim community.
